solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Bribe reserve, otherwise last in pavilion

parts.note: a reserve player is a sub
or means otherwise, as in 'hurry or you'll be late'

indicators.note: last in asks for the final letter of the word pavilion

explanation.surface: A cricket club fixer tries to buy off a reserve player, or else the last man in.
explanation.definitionFit: To suborn someone is to induce them by bribery to do wrong, so it is a verb synonym.

clue.text: I also worried about Conservative Party?

indicators.note: about places the shuffled letters around the next piece
worried suggests agitation, so the letters of I also are churned

explanation.surface: Someone frets about whether the Conservative Party will survive, as they do too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges I ALSO to SOIAL; 'about' puts that round C, giving SO-C-IAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A social is an informal party or gathering, a noun sense hinted by the question mark.

clue.text: One serving Arthur during drunken spree

indicators.note: during means one thing happens within another, so a piece sits inside

parts.note: a bender is a drinking binge
Art is the short form of the name Arthur

explanation.surface: A man named Arthur pours drinks while everyone else is on a drunken binge.
explanation.definitionFit: A bartender is someone who serves drinks at a bar, so 'one serving' describes the job.

clue.text: Stop female artist wearing check

indicators.note: wearing means the next pieces are clothed by the outer word

parts.note: to rein is to check or hold back
RA, Royal Academician, stands for an artist

explanation.surface: Someone tells a woman painter to stop wearing a check pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: RA is a Royal Academician, a member of Britain's Royal Academy of Arts and the crossword's usual artist.
explanation.definitionFit: To refrain is to stop oneself or hold back from doing something, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Poet's on $1,000 for his last work?

parts.note: Shakespeare is the Swan of Avon, so the poet's is swan's
a grand, a thousand dollars, is G

explanation.surface: A poet is paid a thousand dollars for what turns out to be his final piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's nickname 'the Swan of Avon' lets a swan stand for a poet; G for a grand is slang for $1,000.
explanation.definitionFit: A swansong is a final performance or work, from the legend that swans sing just before dying.

clue.text: Entertain in rhyme

parts.note: a phrase for treating someone lavishly to food and drink, whose two halves rhyme with each other

explanation.definitionFit: To wine and dine someone is to entertain them generously with food and drink; the two verbs rhyme.

clue.text: Words of admonishment at this time, and at that time

parts.note: now means at this present time
then means at that past time

explanation.surface: A scolding parent mixes present and past tense while telling a child off.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a mild reproof said to someone misbehaving, as in a gentle warning.

clue.text: Being broadcast from Verona, I reported

indicators.note: reported means the extracted letters are spoken, giving a word that sounds alike
from tells us to take letters out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A reporter files a live piece from the Italian city of Verona.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' pulls ONAI out of veRONA I; 'reported' says it aloud, and in British speech ON A I sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A programme on air is being transmitted live on radio or television.

clue.text: Cutting-edge inventor?

parts.note: reads as a pioneering innovator, but literally the man who invented a blade with a cutting edge, the safety razor

explanation.definitionFit: King C. Gillette invented the disposable safety razor blade, literally a cutting edge.

clue.text: A drop of rouge in restaurant in appropriate container

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the eatery word

parts.note: a cafe is a small restaurant

indicators.note: a drop of rouge is just its first letter

explanation.surface: A splash of red wine spills in a restaurant, caught in a suitable vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: AR goes inside CAFE after the C, giving C-AR-AFE.
explanation.definitionFit: A carafe is a glass jug for serving wine, so it is a fitting container for rouge.

clue.text: Drink second immediately before dance

indicators.note: before puts the earlier pieces ahead of the next one

parts.note: now means immediately
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone orders a second drink just before going off to a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: A snowball is a British cocktail of advocaat and lemonade.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowball is a cocktail of advocaat and lemonade, so it is an example of a drink.

clue.text: English princess, one leaving port on the Nile Delta

indicators.note: leaving means a piece departs from the longer word

parts.note: Alexandria is the Egyptian port on the Nile Delta
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An English princess sets sail from a port on the Nile Delta.
explanation.definitionFit: Princess Alexandra, a cousin of Queen Elizabeth II, is a member of the British royal family.

clue.text: One over the limit in squash club, perhaps

parts.note: squash is a sweet fruit cordial in Britain, a drink
a driver is a golf club

explanation.surface: A player at a squash club has had one too many.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain squash is also a diluted fruit cordial, so it can be a drink as well as a racket sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A drink-driver is someone driving with alcohol above the legal limit.

clue.text: Crowd in store, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says the word for store is spoken, giving a twin in sound

parts.note: a hoard is a store or stockpile

explanation.surface: A crowd gathers in a shop, or so it sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A horde is a large crowd or throng of people.

clue.text: One didn't mind a barking dog

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so the letters go crazy

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs off a dog that keeps barking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barking' (British slang for mad) rearranges the thirteen letters of ONE DIDN'T MIND A.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dandie Dinmont is a Scottish terrier breed named after a character in a Walter Scott novel.

clue.text: Stubborn old boy elected in republic?

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

indicators.note: in puts the elected word inside the nation word

parts.note: a republic is an example of a state
in means elected, as a party voted in

explanation.surface: A stubborn former pupil wins office in a republic.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a republic is only one kind of nation, so it is an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Obstinate means stubbornly refusing to change one's mind, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Puzzle brings on a vexed moment, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly means the phrase is spoken, so its sound gives the answer

parts.note: vexed means cross and a moment is a tick, so the phrase is a cross tick

explanation.surface: A tricky puzzle leaves the solver cross for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: A tick is British informal for a moment, as in 'just a tick'.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrostic is a word puzzle in which initial letters of lines spell a word.

clue.text: Reprimand men, shirkers

parts.note: to carpet someone is to reprimand them
knights are men in chess

explanation.surface: A boss scolds lazy workers for skiving.
explanation.walkthrough: To carpet is British informal for to reprimand, from being called onto the boss's carpet.
explanation.definitionFit: Carpet knights were soldiers who stayed at home in comfort rather than fighting, hence shirkers.

clue.text: Speak non-stop

definitions.meaning: to ... a thought is to put it into words
an ... train runs without intermediate stops

explanation.definitionFit: Express means to put into words, and also describes a train that runs without stopping.

clue.text: Listen to utter gossip

parts.note: hear means listen
say means utter

explanation.surface: Someone is told to listen to some juicy gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearsay is rumour or information passed on without proof, much like gossip.

clue.text: River cut off any number

parts.note: to sever is to cut off
N stands for an unspecified number in maths

explanation.surface: A river splits off countless channels.
explanation.walkthrough: The Severn is Britain's longest river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Severn is the longest river in Britain, so it is an example of a river.

clue.text: Recorded short, freely available

indicators.note: short means the last letter of the phrase is cut

parts.note: something recorded is on tape

explanation.surface: Recordings are briefly made available to all.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on tap is readily available whenever wanted, like beer from a barrel.

clue.text: Subject — best one college offers

parts.note: top means best
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A leading college offers its finest subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is a subject of discussion or study, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Cross-question again former French friend framed by Frenchman

indicators.note: framed by means the pieces sit within the outer name

parts.note: Rene is a typical French man's name
ex means former
ami is French for friend

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's former friend is grilled once more.
explanation.definitionFit: To cross-question a witness again is to put further questions to them after earlier examination.

clue.text: Liable to tip over, have toy piano repaired

indicators.note: repaired suggests putting things back together in a new order

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

explanation.surface: A broken toy piano wobbles and needs fixing.
explanation.definitionFit: Top-heavy means heavier at the top than the base, and so unstable and liable to topple.

clue.text: Large piece of land in eastern nation

parts.note: a state is a nation

explanation.surface: A big plot of land lies in an eastern country.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is an extensive area of land owned by one person or family.

clue.text: Mate's certainly arrogant

parts.note: cock is British informal for mate, a friend; the 's reads as 'is' and joins
sure means certainly

explanation.surface: A friend is undoubtedly full of himself.
explanation.walkthrough: Cock, like mate, is a British informal form of address for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Cocksure means overconfident and conceited, a synonym for arrogant.

clue.text: Fictitious monster with very unusual name

indicators.note: unusual signals the letters of very in an odd order

explanation.surface: A mythical beast bears a very strange name.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a heraldic two-legged winged dragon, a mythical creature.
